title: The Complex Plane
description: Numbers with real and imaginary parts

concepts.title: Complex Numbers and the Argand Plane
concepts.contentHtml:
A complex number has the form z = a + bi, where a is the real part, b is the imaginary part, and i is the square root of -1.

The Argand plane (or complex plane) plots complex numbers as points: the horizontal axis is the real part, the vertical axis is the imaginary part. So z = 3 + 2i sits at the point (3, 2).

This simple idea -- treating numbers as points in a plane -- unlocks an entire universe of mathematics that is impossibly beautiful.

concepts.title: Polar Form and Euler's Formula
concepts.contentHtml:
Every complex number can also be written in polar form: z = re^{i\theta}, where r = |z| is the modulus (distance from origin) and \theta is the argument (angle from positive real axis).

Euler's formula is one of the most stunning equations in mathematics:

e^{i\theta} = cos(\theta) + i sin(\theta)

Setting \theta = \pi gives Euler's identity: e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0, which ties together five fundamental constants.

concepts.title: Complex Arithmetic as Geometry
concepts.contentHtml:
Addition of complex numbers works like vector addition -- it follows the parallelogram rule. Adding z_1 + z_2 means placing the arrows tip-to-tail.

Multiplication is where things get magical. To multiply z_1 \cdot z_2 in polar form: multiply the moduli and add the arguments. Multiplication rotates and scales!

This means multiplying by i rotates a number 90 degrees counterclockwise. Multiplying by -1 rotates 180 degrees. The geometry of complex multiplication is the key to everything that follows.

concepts.title: Functions from C to C
concepts.contentHtml:
A complex function f: C -> C takes a complex number as input and produces a complex number as output. We write f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y), where u and v are real-valued functions of two variables.

Since both input and output live in a plane, a complex function is a transformation of the plane. Every point gets moved to a new location. Visualizing these transformations reveals stunning geometric patterns.

For example, f(z) = z^2 doubles angles and squares distances from the origin. A grid of squares becomes a grid of curved regions.

concepts.title: Key Complex Functions
concepts.contentHtml:
Powers: z^2 doubles angles, z^3 triples them. The map z^n wraps the plane around itself n times.

Inversion: 1/z inverts distances and reflects across the real axis. Points near 0 fly to infinity and vice versa.

Exponential: e^z maps vertical lines to circles and horizontal lines to rays. It's periodic with period 2\pi i!

Trig functions: sin(z) and cos(z) extend to complex inputs and become unbounded -- unlike their real counterparts.

concepts.title: Domain Coloring
concepts.contentHtml:
Domain coloring is a way to visualize complex functions. Since the output is a complex number, we encode it as a color: the hue represents the argument (angle), and the brightness represents the modulus (size).

Zeros appear as points where all colors meet (like a pinwheel). Poles appear as bright white spots surrounded by swirling colors.

Domain coloring reveals the deep structure of complex functions at a glance -- the patterns of zeros, poles, and symmetries become visually obvious.

concepts.title: Complex Differentiability
concepts.contentHtml:
A complex function f is differentiable at z_0 if the limit of [f(z) - f(z_0)]/(z - z_0) exists as z -> z_0. This looks just like the real definition, but there's a crucial difference.

In the real case, x can only approach x_0 from the left or right. In the complex plane, z can approach z_0 from any direction -- and the limit must be the same from every direction!

This makes complex differentiability a vastly stronger condition than real differentiability. Functions that are complex differentiable have almost magical properties.

concepts.title: The Cauchy-Riemann Equations
concepts.contentHtml:
Write f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y). For f to be complex differentiable, the real and imaginary parts must satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations:

These equations say that the partial derivatives of u and v are locked together in a very specific way. They're the algebraic expression of the requirement that the derivative must be the same from every direction.

Most "nice" real functions fail the Cauchy-Riemann equations when extended to C. For instance, f(z) = conjugate(z) = x - iy is smooth but nowhere complex differentiable!
mathExpressions: \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}

concepts.title: Analytic Implies Infinitely Differentiable
concepts.contentHtml:
A function that is complex differentiable in a region is called analytic (or holomorphic). Here's the stunning fact:

If a complex function is differentiable once, it is automatically differentiable infinitely many times! This is wildly different from real analysis, where a function can be differentiable once but not twice.

Moreover, the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic: they satisfy Laplace's equation. This connects complex analysis to physics -- electrostatics, fluid flow, and heat conduction.

concepts.title: Path Integrals in the Complex Plane
concepts.contentHtml:
A contour integral integrates a complex function along a curve (contour) in the complex plane. We write the integral of f(z) dz along a path gamma.

Unlike real integrals which give a number on a number line, contour integrals can depend on which path you take between two points -- not just the endpoints themselves.

The key question of complex analysis: for which functions and domains does the integral depend only on the endpoints?

concepts.title: Cauchy's Integral Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Cauchy's integral theorem: If f is analytic on and inside a closed contour gamma, then the integral around that contour is zero.

This is extraordinary. It means that for analytic functions on simply connected domains, the integral along any closed loop is zero. You can deform the path however you like (without crossing singularities) and the integral doesn't change.

This is the foundation of all of complex analysis. Everything else flows from this single, beautiful result.

concepts.title: Cauchy's Integral Formula
concepts.contentHtml:
Cauchy's integral formula is perhaps the most magical result in all of analysis. It says that the value of an analytic function at any point is completely determined by its values on a surrounding contour:

Think about what this means: knowing f on a circle tells you f everywhere inside the circle. The interior values are "encoded" in the boundary values. This is unique to complex analysis -- nothing like it exists for real functions.

The formula also gives us all higher derivatives for free!

concepts.title: Types of Singularities
concepts.contentHtml:
A singularity of f is a point where f is not analytic. There are three types:

Removable: The function has a finite limit at the point. Example: sin(z)/z at z = 0 (limit is 1). You can "fill in" the hole.

Pole: The function blows up like 1/(z - z_0)^n. A pole of order n means (z - z_0)^n f(z) has a removable singularity.

Essential: Everything else. The function goes haywire near the point -- not approaching infinity in any organized way.

concepts.title: Laurent Series
concepts.contentHtml:
A Laurent series is like a Taylor series but with negative powers too. Around a singularity z_0, we write f as a sum of terms with both positive and negative powers of (z - z_0).

The negative-power part is called the principal part. It encodes the singularity's behavior: a removable singularity has no negative powers, a pole of order n has finitely many (down to (z - z_0)^{-n}), and an essential singularity has infinitely many negative powers.

The coefficient of 1/(z - z_0) is especially important -- it's called the residue.

concepts.title: Picard's Great Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Near a pole, a function just blows up to infinity. But near an essential singularity, something extraordinary happens.

Picard's Great Theorem: In any neighborhood of an essential singularity, an analytic function takes every complex value infinitely often, with at most one exception!

For example, e^{1/z} near z = 0: in any tiny disc around 0, the function takes every value except 0 infinitely many times. The function oscillates so wildly that it covers almost the entire complex plane infinitely often in any neighborhood.

concepts.title: The Residue Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
The Residue Theorem is the crown jewel of complex analysis. It says that a contour integral around a closed curve equals 2\pi i times the sum of all the residues inside:

This is incredibly powerful. Instead of computing a difficult integral directly, you just need to find the singularities inside the contour and compute their residues -- often a much easier calculation.

The theorem unifies Cauchy's integral theorem (no singularities means the integral is zero) and Cauchy's integral formula (one simple pole gives the function value).

concepts.title: Real Integrals via Complex Methods
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the most magical applications: computing real integrals using complex analysis. Many integrals that seem impossible by real methods yield easily to contour integration.

The classic example: to compute the integral from 0 to infinity of 1/(1 + x^2) dx, we integrate 1/(1 + z^2) around a semicircular contour in the upper half-plane. The pole at z = i has residue 1/(2i), and the semicircular arc contributes zero as the radius goes to infinity.

Result: the integral equals pi/2. A difficult real calculus problem becomes an elegant residue computation.

concepts.title: Evaluating Sums Using Residues
concepts.contentHtml:
Residues can also evaluate infinite series. The trick: the function pi cot(pi z) has simple poles at every integer with residue 1.

By integrating f(z) pi cot(pi z) around a large contour and using the residue theorem, you can relate the sum of f(n) over all integers to the residues of f itself.

For example, this technique shows that the sum of 1/n^2 from n = 1 to infinity equals pi^2/6 -- the famous Basel problem, first solved by Euler.
mathExpressions: \text{Res}(\pi \cot(\pi z), n) = 1 \text{ for each integer } n

concepts.title: Conformal Maps Preserve Angles
concepts.contentHtml:
An analytic function with nonzero derivative is conformal: it preserves angles between curves. Two curves meeting at an angle alpha will still meet at angle alpha after applying the map.

This means conformal maps distort sizes but not shapes -- at least locally. Tiny circles get mapped to tiny circles (not ellipses). Tiny squares get mapped to tiny squares. The local geometry is preserved.

This property makes conformal maps invaluable in physics and engineering wherever angle-preservation matters.
mathExpressions: f'(z_0) \neq 0 \implies f \text{ is conformal at } z_0

concepts.title: Mobius Transformations
concepts.contentHtml:
Mobius transformations (linear fractional transformations) have the form f(z) = (az + b)/(cz + d) where ad - bc is nonzero. They are the most important conformal maps.

Key property: Mobius transformations map circles and lines to circles and lines. (Lines are "circles through infinity.")

They form a group under composition. Any Mobius transformation is determined by where it sends three points -- and you can always find one sending any three points to any other three points.

concepts.title: The Riemann Mapping Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
The Riemann Mapping Theorem is one of the most profound results in complex analysis:

Any simply connected open subset of C (other than C itself) can be mapped conformally onto the open unit disk.

This means all simply connected regions are conformally equivalent! A weird amoeba-shaped region, a half-plane, a strip -- they can all be conformally mapped to the unit disk. The theorem is purely existential; finding the actual map is usually very hard.

Applications: In fluid dynamics, you solve a problem on the disk (easy) and map back to the complicated region. Same for electrostatics and heat flow.

title: Riemann Surfaces & Beyond
description: Multi-valued functions and the Riemann sphere

concepts.title: Multi-Valued Functions
concepts.contentHtml:
Some complex functions are naturally multi-valued. The square root sqrt(z) has two values for every z. The logarithm log(z) has infinitely many values, differing by multiples of 2\pi i.

To make these functions well-defined, we introduce branch cuts: curves in the complex plane where we "cut" to prevent going around a singularity and arriving at a different value.

For sqrt(z), a branch cut along the negative real axis gives a single-valued function on the rest of the plane. But this feels artificial -- surely there's a better way?

concepts.title: Riemann Surfaces
concepts.contentHtml:
A Riemann surface is a geometric construction that makes multi-valued functions single-valued. Instead of cutting the plane, we let it have multiple "sheets" connected at branch points.

For sqrt(z): take two copies of the complex plane, cut each along the negative real axis, and glue the top edge of one to the bottom edge of the other. The result is a surface where sqrt(z) is perfectly single-valued.

Riemann surfaces are some of the most beautiful objects in mathematics. They connect complex analysis, topology, and algebraic geometry in profound ways.

concepts.title: The Riemann Sphere and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
The Riemann sphere is the complex plane plus a single point at infinity: C union {infinity}. Topologically, it's a sphere -- we wrap the complex plane around a ball using stereographic projection.

On the Riemann sphere, Mobius transformations become rotations and distortions of the sphere. Poles are just points where a function "equals infinity" -- no more special than zeros.

From here, complex analysis connects to: algebraic geometry (Riemann surfaces are algebraic curves), string theory (strings sweep out Riemann surfaces in spacetime), and the Riemann Hypothesis -- perhaps the greatest unsolved problem in mathematics, about the zeros of the Riemann zeta function.
